title: Why diversification works
objectives: Compute the variance of a two-asset portfolio and find when mixing lowers risk.

screens.title: Splitting the money
screens.prose: Funds X and Y each return +20% or −20%, with chance 1/2, independently. You put half your money in each. Each cell shows the mix's return.
screens.question: Compared with holding one fund, how spread out is the 50:50 mix's return?

options.text: Just as spread out: each fund swings 20%
options.why: You averaged the two funds' swings. Half the time they disagree, and then the mix returns 0%.

options.text: More spread out: two funds, two sources of risk
options.why: You added the risks. Each fund is only half the money, and their swings partly cancel.

hints.text: Look at the two off-diagonal cells.
When the funds disagree, the mix returns 0%.
One fund alone is always 20% from its mean; the mix is 20% away only half the time.

feedback.correct: Half the time the funds cancel and the mix returns 0%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what the mix returns when the funds disagree.

explain.text: One fund alone always lands 20% from its mean of 0%. The mix lands there only when both agree, chance 1/2. Otherwise the swings cancel to 0%.

screens.title: Diversification
screens.prose: Lowering risk by mixing assets that do not move in lockstep is **diversification**. The mix returns −20% or +20% with chance 1/4 each, and 0% with chance 1/2.
screens.question: What is the standard deviation of the mix's return?

hints.text: The mean is 0. Square each return as a decimal: $0.2^2 = 0.04$.
Variance $= 0.04 \times \tfrac{1}{4} + 0 \times \tfrac{1}{2} + 0.04 \times \tfrac{1}{4}$.
The variance is 0.02. Take the square root.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the variance from the three outcomes, then take the root.

byKey.avg: You averaged the two funds' sds. The mix lands at 0% half the time, so its sd is smaller.
byKey.half: You halved the sd. Half of each fund halves each sd, but the two halves add as variances: $\sqrt{0.01 + 0.01}$.
byKey.var: That is the variance, 0.02. The sd is its square root.

explain.text: The variance is $0.04 \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 0.02$, so the sd is 14.14%, down from 20%. That is $20\% / \sqrt{2}$. Each half has variance $0.25 \times 0.04$, and independent variances add.

screens.title: Weight and correlation
screens.prose: Now X and Y each have sd 20%, with correlation $\rho$. You hold $w$ in X and $1 - w$ in Y. The curve is the portfolio variance. Move both sliders.

derive.caption: $w$ = {{fixed(w, 2)}}: variance {{fixed(w*w*sx*sx + (1 - w)*(1 - w)*sy*sy + 2*w*(1 - w)*r*sx*sy, 4)}}, sd {{fixed(sqrt(max(0, w*w*sx*sx + (1 - w)*(1 - w)*sy*sy + 2*w*(1 - w)*r*sx*sy)) * 100, 2)}}%

screens.question: Set $\rho = 1$. What happens to the curve?

options.text: It goes flat at 0.04: no mix is safer than one fund
It still dips at 50:50, just less
options.why: You expected some benefit from any mix. At $\rho = 1$ the funds move in lockstep, so nothing cancels.
That happens at $\rho = -1$. At $+1$ the swings line up instead of cancelling.

hints.text: Drag $\rho$ all the way to the right.
Compare the curve with the line for Y alone.

feedback.correct: At $\rho = 1$ every mix has the same 20% sd.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $\rho = 1$ and look at the whole curve.

explain.text: At $\rho = 1$ the two funds always move together, so mixing them just holds 20% risk. At $\rho = 0$ the 50:50 mix has variance 0.02. At $\rho = -1$ it falls to 0: the swings cancel exactly.

screens.title: Perfect cancelling
screens.prose: New funds: X has sd 30%, Y has sd 10%, and $\rho = -1$. When X rises, Y falls, always.

derive.caption: $w$ = {{fixed(w, 2)}}: variance {{fixed(w*w*sx*sx + (1 - w)*(1 - w)*sy*sy + 2*w*(1 - w)*r*sx*sy, 4)}}, sd {{fixed(sqrt(max(0, w*w*sx*sx + (1 - w)*(1 - w)*sy*sy + 2*w*(1 - w)*r*sx*sy)) * 100, 2)}}%

screens.question: Set $w$ to the weight in X that removes all risk.

hints.text: The curve touches 0 at one weight.
X swings three times as far as Y.
Hold three times as much Y as X: $w = 0.25$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the curve touches 0.

byKey.half: You split 50:50. X swings three times as far as Y, so equal money does not cancel.
byKey.allY: Y alone still has 10% sd. A little X cancels its swings.

explain.text: With $w = 0.25$, X contributes $0.25 \times 30\% = 7.5\%$ swings and Y $0.75 \times 10\% = 7.5\%$, in opposite directions. They cancel exactly. That is a perfect hedge.

screens.title: Going short
screens.prose: Same sds, 30% and 10%, but now $\rho = 0.8$. A negative $w$ means you short X and put more than all your money in Y.

derive.caption: $w$ = {{fixed(w, 2)}}: variance {{fixed(w*w*sx*sx + (1 - w)*(1 - w)*sy*sy + 2*w*(1 - w)*r*sx*sy, 4)}}, sd {{fixed(sqrt(max(0, w*w*sx*sx + (1 - w)*(1 - w)*sy*sy + 2*w*(1 - w)*r*sx*sy)) * 100, 2)}}%

screens.question: Set $w$ to the weight with the lowest variance.

hints.text: Start at $w = 0$, Y alone, and move left.
The curve keeps falling below the Y-alone line for negative $w$.
The lowest point is near $w = -0.27$.

feedback.correct: About $-0.27$: short 27% in X, 127% in Y.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the lowest point, left of 0.

byKey.allY: You stopped at Y alone. With $\rho = 0.8$, shorting a little X cancels part of Y's swings.
byKey.long: Any long X adds risk here: X is riskier and moves with Y.

explain.text: The lowest point is at $w \approx -0.27$, with sd 7.89%, below Y's 10%. Shorting X cancels part of Y's swings because they move together. When $\rho$ is high, the safest mix can need a short position.

screens.title: Averaging the sds
screens.prose: Funds with sds 30% and 10%, correlation 0.2. A colleague says the 50:50 mix has sd 20%, the average of the two.
screens.question: What is the sd of the 50:50 mix?

hints.text: Use $w^2\sigma_X^2 + (1 - w)^2\sigma_Y^2 + 2w(1 - w)\rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y$.
The three terms are $0.0225$, $0.0025$ and $2 \times 0.25 \times 0.2 \times 0.03$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the three variance terms, then take the root.

byKey.avg: You averaged the sds. That is right only when $\rho = 1$; at 0.2 the swings partly cancel.
byKey.nocov: You left out the cross term $2w(1 - w)\rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y = 0.003$.
byKey.var: That is the variance. Take the root.
byKey.onecov: You used $w(1 - w)\rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y$ once. The cross term counts it twice.

explain.text: The terms are $0.0225 + 0.0025 + 0.003 = 0.028$, so the sd is 16.73%. Averaging sds assumes $\rho = 1$, when nothing cancels. Below 1, the mix is always safer than the average.

screens.title: The portfolio formula
screens.prose: Derive the formula you used. The portfolio is $P = wX + (1 - w)Y$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\operatorname{Var}(P) = w^2\sigma_X^2 + (1 - w)^2\sigma_Y^2 + 2w(1 - w)\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)$, take $E$ term by term

hints.text: Start from the definition of variance.
Write the distance $P - \mu_P$ before squaring it.
Definition, distance, square, expectation, correlation.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build the distance first, then square it, then average.

byKey.sq: Square the distance only after writing it out.

explain.text: The first two terms are each fund's own risk, scaled by its weight squared. The cross term carries the correlation. Diversification lives in that term: it shrinks as $\rho$ falls.

screens.title: The lowest point
screens.prose: Setting the derivative in $w$ to zero gives the minimum-variance weight: $$w^* = \frac{\sigma_Y^2 - \rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y}{\sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2 - 2\rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y}.$$ Multivariable calculus, lesson 12, derived it with a Lagrange multiplier.
screens.question: With $\sigma_X = 0.25$, $\sigma_Y = 0.15$ and $\rho = 0.4$, what is $w^*$?

hints.text: $\rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y = 0.4 \times 0.25 \times 0.15 = 0.015$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $\rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y$ first, then the top and bottom.

byKey.swap: You put $\sigma_X^2$ on top. That gives the weight in Y, $1 - w^*$.
byKey.norho: You left out the $\rho$ terms. With $\rho = 0.4$ they matter.

explain.text: $w^* = 0.0075/0.055 \approx 0.136$: about 14% in the riskier X. Even a riskier asset earns a place when $\rho$ is below $\sigma_Y/\sigma_X = 0.6$. Above that, $w^*$ turns negative, as on the short-selling screen.

screens.title: Many assets
screens.prose: Hold $n$ assets equally, each with sd 30%, every pair with correlation 0.2. Then $$\operatorname{Var} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} + \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)\rho\sigma^2.$$ The curve is the portfolio's sd.
screens.question: As $n$ grows without limit, what sd does the portfolio approach?

hints.text: What happens to $\sigma^2/n$ as $n$ grows?
It vanishes, and $1 - 1/n$ goes to 1.
The variance tends to $\rho\sigma^2 = 0.2 \times 0.09 = 0.018$. Take the root.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Let $n$ grow in the formula: one term vanishes, one stays.

byKey.zero: You expected diversification to remove all risk. That needs $\rho = 0$, the dashed curve.
byKey.var: That is the variance floor. Take its root.
byKey.rhosd: You multiplied $\rho$ by $\sigma$. The floor is on the variance: $\sqrt{\rho\sigma^2}$.
byKey.thirty: That is 30 assets. The limit is a little lower.

explain.text: The own-risk term $\sigma^2/n$ falls like $1/n$, but the shared term floors at $\rho\sigma^2 = 0.018$. So the sd never drops below 13.42%. Risk every asset shares cannot be diversified away.

screens.title: A two-fund portfolio
screens.prose: You hold £60,000 in an equity fund and £40,000 in a bond fund. Over a year their returns have these sds, with correlation 0.2.
screens.question: What is the sd of the portfolio's yearly P&L, in £?

hints.text: Work in £: each fund's P&L sd is in the last column.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two variances and the cross term, then take the root.

byKey.sds: You added the two sds. That assumes $\rho = 1$; at 0.2 the risks partly cancel.
byKey.nocov: You left out the cross term. With $\rho = 0.2$ it adds £10.4 million in £².
byKey.var: That is the variance, in £². Take its root.

explain.text: The variance is 132,768,000 £², so the sd is about £11,522. Adding the sds would say £13,200. Most of the risk is the equity fund; the bonds add little and partly cancel.

screens.title: Why an index fund still moves
screens.prose: An index fund holds 500 stocks about equally. Each has sd 30% a year, and a typical pair has correlation 0.3.
screens.question: What is the index fund's sd?

hints.text: Add the two parts of the variance.
Take the square root.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two parts, then take the root.

byKey.indep: You treated the stocks as independent, $30\%/\sqrt{500}$. They share market moves, so the variance floors at $\rho\sigma^2$.
byKey.one: That is one stock. 500 stocks remove almost all of each one's own risk.
byKey.var: That is the variance. Take its root.

explain.text: The own-risk part, 0.00018, is almost gone; the shared part, 0.027, remains. So the index has an sd near 16.5%, like real broad equity indices. Index funds remove idiosyncratic risk, never market risk.

ideas: A mix's variance is each asset's weighted variance plus a cross term that carries the correlation.
Below $\rho = 1$ the mix is safer than the average of the sds; at $\rho = -1$ it can be riskless.
With many assets, own risk falls like $1/n$, but shared risk floors at $\rho\sigma^2$.
summary.trap: Averaging the sds is right only at $\rho = 1$, where mixing gives no benefit at all.

quiz.prose: Two independent assets each have sd 10%. You hold them 50:50.
quiz.question: What is the portfolio's sd?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add $w^2\sigma^2$ for each asset, then take the root.

byKey.avg: You averaged the sds. That assumes $\rho = 1$.
byKey.half: You halved the sd. The two halves add as variances.
byKey.var: That is the variance. Take its root.

explain.text: Each half has variance $0.25 \times 0.01 = 0.0025$. Together 0.005, so the sd is 7.07%.

quiz.prose: Assets with sds 30% and 10% have correlation exactly 1. You hold them 50:50.
quiz.question: What is the portfolio's sd?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $\rho = 1$ the variance is a perfect square.

byKey.nocov: You left out the cross term. At $\rho = 1$ it is as large as it can be.
byKey.var: That is the variance. Take its root.
byKey.low: You expected the mix to beat the calmer asset. At $\rho = 1$ nothing cancels.

explain.text: At $\rho = 1$, $\operatorname{Var} = (0.5 \times 0.3 + 0.5 \times 0.1)^2 = 0.04$. So the sd is 20%, the plain average.

quiz.prose: Four independent assets each have sd 20%. You hold each with weight 1/4.
quiz.question: What is the portfolio's sd?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The variance falls like $1/n$, so the sd like $1/\sqrt{n}$.

byKey.linear: You divided the sd by 4. The variance falls by 4, so the sd by 2.
byKey.same: That is one asset. Independent assets partly cancel.
byKey.var: That is the variance. Take its root.

explain.text: $\operatorname{Var} = 4 \times \tfrac{1}{16} \times 0.04 = 0.01$, so the sd is 10%. Four assets halve the risk.

quiz.prose: Two assets have the same sd. You will hold them 50:50.
quiz.question: Which correlation gives the lowest portfolio risk?

options.why: You took independence as the best case. Negative correlation cancels more.
You picked the case with no benefit. At $\rho = 1$ the assets move in lockstep.

feedback.correct: At $\rho = -1$ the 50:50 mix has zero risk.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which $\rho$ makes the cross term most negative?

explain.text: The cross term is $2w(1 - w)\rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y$. It is most negative at $\rho = -1$, where equal swings cancel exactly.
